entries.text: screen readers: jaws, narrator, and nvda skip to main content foundational assistive technology manual screen readers: jaws, narrator, and nvda choose one screen reader and learn the same workplace skills with product-specific commands. all manuals ten screen readers lessons my progress start screen readers lesson 1 screen readers final quiz and certificate first-time keyboard guide use this short routine before following the screen readers: jaws, narrator, and nvda procedures. it explains exactly how the keyboard directions in this manual work. press a single key find the named key without pressing it if possible. press and release the key one time. do not hold it unless the step specifically says to hold it. stop and listen to the full screen-reader announcement before pressing another key. press a keyboard combination when a command contains a plus sign, such as ctrl+s, hold down the first key. while continuing to hold the first key, press and release the final key once. release the first key. the plus sign is not a key and should not be pressed. listen for the expected result described in the procedure. if nothing changes, verify that the correct application or webpage has focus and try the command once more. press a sequence of keys when keys are separated by commas or the word “then,” press and release them in order instead of holding them together. after each key, listen for a menu, tab, control, or new screen before continuing. if the announcement does not match the step, press escape once to close the current menu or dialog and restart that procedure. know which navigation key to try tab and shift+tab: move forward and backward among buttons, links, fields, and other controls. arrow keys: move inside menus, lists, groups of choices, text, and many screen-reader reading views. enter: opens the selected

entries.text: brailleblaster accessible manual skip to main content accessible technology manual brailleblaster accessible manual a keyboard-first guide for blind and low-vision learners using jaws. all manuals ten brailleblaster lessons my progress start brailleblaster lesson 1 brailleblaster final quiz and certificate first-time keyboard guide use this short routine before following the brailleblaster accessible manual procedures. it explains exactly how the keyboard directions in this manual work. press a single key find the named key without pressing it if possible. press and release the key one time. do not hold it unless the step specifically says to hold it. stop and listen to the full screen-reader announcement before pressing another key. press a keyboard combination when a command contains a plus sign, such as ctrl+s, hold down the first key. while continuing to hold the first key, press and release the final key once. release the first key. the plus sign is not a key and should not be pressed. listen for the expected result described in the procedure. if nothing changes, verify that the correct application or webpage has focus and try the command once more. press a sequence of keys when keys are separated by commas or the word “then,” press and release them in order instead of holding them together. after each key, listen for a menu, tab, control, or new screen before continuing. if the announcement does not match the step, press escape once to close the current menu or dialog and restart that procedure. know which navigation key to try tab and shift+tab: move forward and backward among buttons, links, fields, and other controls. arrow keys: move inside menus, lists, groups of choices, text, and many screen-reader reading views. enter: opens the selected item or activates the focused command. space: activ

entries.title: Thunderbird Email Keyboard Manual
entries.snippet: Skip to main content Full course manual Thunderbird Email Keyboard Manual Build an independent email routine on Windows, one task at a time. Start Lesson 1 All ten lessons Final quiz and certificate Back to all manuals · Search learning resources This manual c
entries.text: thunderbird email keyboard manual skip to main content full course manual thunderbird email keyboard manual build an independent email routine on windows, one task at a time. start lesson 1 all ten lessons final quiz and certificate back to all manuals · search learning resources this manual covers the thunderbird desktop application on windows, not thunderbird for android. use your usual screen reader. commands were checked against mozilla documentation on september 17, 2026; the procedures have not been tested here with jaws, nvda, or narrator on windows. names and announcements can vary by version, account provider, and layout. first-time learner: how to follow a task before you begin email terms before you start install and open thunderbird on windows 1. connect an existing email account 2. find your place and read a message 3. write, review, and save a draft 4. add and verify a practice attachment 5. find a message without losing the rest of your inbox 6. archive a message and locate it again 7. troubleshooting practice 8. independent practice tasks address a message: to, cc, and bcc send to yourself, reply, and forward a repeatable mailbox routine keyboard command reference — windows sources and next steps practice this topic in mission control first-time learner: how to follow a task read the task title and its starting location before pressing anything. a keyboard command acts on the active application and focused control. merely having these instructions visible does not make the other application active. keep these instructions available. open the application separately. on windows, hold alt, tap tab to choose its window, and release alt. check the window title before continuing. focus is the place receiving your next keystroke. a screen reader announces its name and role; a visible border or highlight may mark it. tab selects the next keyboard-accessible control. shift+tab reverses that movement. neither command means “activate.” at a button or link, press enter to activate. a checkbox is an on/off choice: space changes it. listen for checked or not checked. in an open menu, use arrows to select an item, then enter. escape usually closes that menu; it does not universally return to the previous page. at a text field, enter only the requested information. ctrl+a selects all text in that field ; typing then replaces it. confirm focus before doing this. use left and right to review a small correction, or backspace to remove the character before the cursor. after opening a dialog, listen to its title, read its instructions, and tab through its controls. use cancel if you are unsure. do not repeatedly activate a button while a page or file is loading. at the result checkpoint, stop. say what changed. if the result is different, use that task’s recovery paragraph before attempting the next task. with a screen reader, arrow-key reading and text editing can use different modes. if letters become navigation commands instead of text, confirm you reached an editable field and consult your reader’s forms/focus-mode instructions in the screen readers manual . do not turn the reader off to solve an unidentified focus problem. when a task says to locate a named control, start with tab or shift+tab and listen to each complete label and role. tab skips ordinary paragraphs. if the page itself needs to be read, use your screen reader’s reading commands. if you pass the same controls twice without finding the requested one, stop and check the application, page, account, and open dialogs. a fixed number of tab presses is unreliable because layouts change. recording progress: write down the task, your starting location, the result, and one step to practice again. these activities are optional and repeatable; they are not a sequence of locked lessons. before you begin you need thunderbird installed, an existing email account, an internet connection for account setup and sending, and access to your provider's sign-in verification method. on a workplace computer, ask your technology team whether this email application is permitted before connecting a work account. begin with a personal practice account or a draft with no recipient. use made-up practice content. do not use client records in exercises. read the keyboard directions a plus sign means hold the modifier while pressing the final key. for ctrl+shift+a, hold control and shift, tap a, then release all three. do not type the plus sign. “then” means separate actions. pause after each action and listen before continuing. if your laptop uses function keys for volume or brightness, you may need its fn key. tab moves among controls; shift+tab moves backward. follow the announced control names instead of counting a fixed number of tab presses. read this manual in your browser, then switch to thunderbird before practicing. a command sent to the browser can do something entirely different. for screen-reader modes and recovery, review the screen readers manual and recovery manual . email terms before you start email provider and thunderbird your provider operates your mailbox. thunderbird is an application for accessing it; installing thunderbird does not create an email address. account, folder, and message an account is a mailbox identity. its folders organize messages. select the account’s inbox before choosing a message; two accounts can each have an inbox. draft, sent, and outbox a draft is unfinished mail. sent normally stores a copy after sending. an outbox can contain mail waiting to be sent. a saved draft is not evidence of delivery. attachment a separate file included with a message. its filename is different from the subject. check both before sending. thread a grouped conversation. a collapsed thread can conceal replies; expand it with the list’s available controls before concluding a reply is missing. install and open thunderbird on windows start here: a supported windows computer, an internet connection, and permission to install applications. have your existing email address available. step-by-step instructions open your browser. go to thunderbird’s official website . locate its download option and choose the windows installer. do not use a sponsored download site. after the download finishes, open the installer from your browser’s downloads list. read the windows permission prompt. continue only if it identifies the application you intended to install; a managed device may require your technology team. follow the installer’s labeled next or install controls. leave options you do not understand at their defaults. finish the installation and open thunderbird. if thunderbird is installed already, press the windows key, type thunderbird, review the matching application name, and press enter. continue with “connect an existing email account” below. check your result the thunderbird application is open. you may see account setup instead of a mailbox on the first launch. if something goes wrong a browser tab showing thunderbird’s website is not the installed application. use the windows application search to verify. if installation is blocked, retain the error and ask the device administrator. try it yourself point out which window is the browser and which is thunderbird before entering account information. documentation: mozilla installation instructions . 1. connect an existing email account what you will learn: connect your account and reach your mailbox without guessing server settings. exactly how to do it open thunderbird. a new installation offers account setup. otherwise, open its application menu and choose new account, then existing email. use tab to reach the menu, enter to open it, and arrow keys to explore. enter the requested display name, complete email address, and password. review each field before moving on. activate continue. wait for the provider configuration results. review the account and connection choices. imap is normally the proposed option. if automatic setup fails, obtain the exact settings from your provider or technology team. activate done when the settings are correct. if your provider opens a sign-in window, complete its authentication and review the requested access. allow time for folders and messages to arrive. what should happen: your account and folders become available. if that does not happen: read the actual sign-in or configuration error before retrying. never replace server names with guesses. source: mozilla account configuration 2. find your place and read a message press f6 to move between major areas; shift+f6 moves backward. find the folder pane. select inbox with arrow keys. move to the message list. choose a message with up or down. press enter to open it. read with your screen reader's reading commands. close the opened message tab with ctrl+w. confirm the mailbox is active before continuing. practice: explain aloud whether you are choosing a folder, choosing a message, or reading its contents. if you cannot name the area, pause rather than issuing a deletion or reply command. source: mozilla keyboard shortcuts 3. write, review, and save a draft start here: thunderbird’s main mail window, with an account connected. this first exercise will not be sent. step-by-step instructions press ctrl+n to open a composition window. confirm that a new message is active, rather than a folder or browser search field. leave to empty for this exercise. tab until subject is announced. type “email practice — draft only.” tab to the editable message body. type a greeting, two practice sentences, and your name. press enter between paragraphs. read back what you wrote using your normal text-reading method. use shift+tab or tab to review subject and the recipient area. confirm that no recipient has accidentally been added. return to the body if you need to correct a sentence. press ctrl+s. wait for saving to finish. close only the composition window with ctrl+w; if asked whether to save changes, choose save. in the main window, use f6 to locate the folder pane. use arrows to reach this account’s drafts folder. move to its message list with f6, select your subject, and open it with enter. verify that the subject and both sentences are still present. save again after any changes. check your result you can reopen your unfinished message. it remains a draft and has not been sent. if something goes wrong if drafts appears empty, check the account and clear any active filter. if the composition window is still open, return there and save again. do not use send to make a draft appear in a folder. try it yourself change one sentence, save, close, and reopen the same draft. explain how saving differs from sending. documentation: writing and saving messages . 4. add and verify a practice attachment start here: an open practice draft and a small, harmless file named email-practice.txt. know the folder containing it. step-by-step instructions press ctrl+shift+a in the composition window. confirm that the file-selection dialog opens. if you know the file’s full path, tab to file name, enter that path, and activate open. otherwise use the dialog’s folder navigation to reach its containing folder, select the filename, and activate open. selecting a folder only navigates; it does not attach a file. back in the draft, locate the attachment area with tab or shift+tab. review the exact filename. if it is the wrong file, select that attachment and use its context menu to remove it. confirm the attachment item has focus before deleting anything. reattach the intended file and save the draft. before sending an actual document, open the original file separately and verify its contents as well as its name. when receiving an attachment, identify its sender, message context, and filename before opening it. use its available save action if you want a local copy; note the destination folder and any rename you make. check your result the draft lists exactly the file you intended. you can distinguish the attached copy from the original file on your computer. if something goes wrong if the file picker says the item cannot be found, check the path and extension. cancel and locate the file in file explorer instead of choosing another similarly named document. large attachments may exceed your provider’s limit. try it yourself attach, remove, and reattach the practice file without deleting its original on disk. documentation: attachment shortcut . 5. find a message without losing the rest of your inbox select the folder you want to search. press ctrl+shift+k to reach quick filter. enter a distinctive subject word or sender name. review the available sender, recipients, subject, and body options. select the fields relevant to your search. check whether unread, starred, or attachment filters are also limiting the results. return to the results and inspect the matching messages. press escape as needed to clear the filter and hide the filter bar. expected result: matching messages appear; clearing the filter restores the broader list. filtering changes which messages you see, not which messages exist. practice: search for “email practice,” then deliberately use a word that is not in your message. explain why an empty result does not prove your mail was deleted. source: mozilla quick filter 6. archive a message and locate it again select one expendable practice message. activate archive, or press a while the message list has focus. find the archive location for that account and locate the message again. archiving moves a message out of its current folder. the destination can be an account folder or a local folder, depending on the account's copies & folders settings. it remains searchable. archiving is not a separate backup. practice: before archiving anything important, demonstrate the complete round trip with your practice message: find it, archive it, and find it again. source: mozilla archived messages 7. troubleshooting practice the command affected my browser. switch to thunderbird, confirm the active window, and try again. typing goes into a search field. identify the focused control before repeating the command. do not assume the message list is active. my message list suddenly looks empty. check the selected folder and clear quick filter before assuming mail is missing. the draft is not in sent. saving and sending are different tasks. look for the draft and review it before sending. my screen reader uses the letter command itself. check focus and your reader's interaction mode. use the corresponding thunderbird menu action if needed. do not turn off speech and continue blindly. i cannot explain an error. record the exact error text, the action immediately before it, and whether it affects one account or all accounts. share that information with your instructor or technology team. 8. independent practice tasks choose any task. there is no required order or passing score. use the instructions again whenever you need them. orientation: find inbox and identify one message's sender and subject. describe your current location. draft: write a three-sentence introduction without a recipient. save it and explain why it has not been sent. attachment: add email-practice.txt and verify the filename. search: find your practice subject, then restore the unfiltered list. recovery: ask an instructor to select a different folder. identify what changed before searching. organization: archive a practice message and retrieve it. after each task, note what you completed independently, what prompt helped, and what you want to repeat. these are practice activities in thunderbird; this manual does not yet add an automated thunderbird mission control lesson. address a message: to, cc, and bcc start here: a new composition window. use only your own address for the first practice. step-by-step instructions tab to the to field. type your complete email address and press enter. the address becomes a recipient item. review its spelling; an accepted-looking item is not proof that the address belongs to the intended person. to add another recipient, enter their address in the same row and confirm with enter. to move onward after the last recipient, press enter again or tab and identify the next field. to correct an existing recipient, use the arrow keys in the recipient row to select that item. press enter to edit it, make the correction, and press enter again. delete removes a selected recipient item. if you need cc or bcc, reach the corresponding control above the address row with tab or shift+tab and activate it. cc recipients are visible to the other recipients. bcc conceals the bcc recipient list from them. before sending, review every recipient row, not only to. in a practice draft, remove added recipients and save without sending. check your result each intended address is a distinct recipient item, and you know which address row it is in. if something goes wrong if a field is absent, activate its cc or bcc control first. if deleting removes message text instead of an address, stop: focus is in the body. return to the recipient row before trying again. try it yourself explain who should see a copy of a hypothetical meeting invitation, then choose to or cc. do not test privacy by mailing real groups. documentation: mozilla recipient addressing . send to yourself, reply, and forward start here: a saved practice draft and your own working email address. step-by-step instructions open the draft, add your own address in to, and review subject, body, and any attachments. remove anything you did not intend to include. press ctrl+enter to send. if a confirmation appears, read it and confirm only when the reviewed message is ready. allow the operation to finish. return to the main mail window and select the account’s sent folder. locate the practice subject. then select inbox and refresh that account with f5 if needed. delivery can take time. open the received practice message. press ctrl+r to reply to its sender. check the recipient before writing a short answer; save the reply as a draft or send it to yourself. for a real group message, ctrl+shift+r opens reply all. review the expanded recipient list before writing. cancel an unnecessary group reply rather than sending it by accident. to forward, open the original practice message and press ctrl+l. add your own address, inspect the quoted material and attached files, and add a sentence explaining why you are forwarding it. save the practice forward as a draft. check your result you can distinguish a newly composed message, a reply, and a forward by checking recipients and content, not just the subject prefix. if something goes wrong a sent copy does not guarantee that someone read a message. if sending reports an error, record it and check the connection and account sign-in. inspect sent and outbox before pressing send repeatedly. try it yourself send yourself one clearly labeled test only. identify its sent copy and its received inbox copy. documentation: thunderbird command reference · sending and receiving . a repeatable mailbox routine start here: the main mail window. choose a practice message that you can safely reorganize. step-by-step instructions identify the account and select inbox. use f6 to reach the message list and arrows to select one message. read its sender and subject before opening it. open it with enter, read it, and decide whether it needs a reply, a later action, or no action. close the message tab with ctrl+w when finished. if you want to distinguish read from unread, select the message in the list and press m once. check the resulting status before pressing again; this command toggles the state. to retain the message outside inbox, archive it using the archive task. to discard only an expendable practice message, select it in the message list and press delete. after an accidental deletion, try ctrl+z immediately. otherwise examine the account’s trash folder and use the message’s context menu to move it back to inbox. do not empty trash during this exercise. finish by clearing any quick filter and checking the selected folder. this leaves a predictable starting point for your next session. check your result you can explain where the practice message went and find it again. if something goes wrong do not use shift+delete for practice: permanent deletion may not be recoverable. if multiple messages are selected unexpectedly, stop and select only the intended item before continuing. try it yourself record the starting folder, action, and destination for one archived message and one discarded test message. documentation: read status, delete, and undo commands · archive behavior . keyboard command reference — windows commands depend on focus. use mail commands in the mail window and composition commands in a draft. core thunderbird shortcuts task command next / previous major area f6 / shift+f6 open selected message enter new message ctrl+n reply to sender ctrl+r reply to everyone ctrl+shift+r forward ctrl+l save draft ctrl+s attach a file ctrl+shift+a quick filter ctrl+shift+k archive selected message a close current tab or window ctrl+w send reviewed message ctrl+enter (composition window) get messages for current account f5 toggle read/unread m (selected message) delete selected message delete undo last supported action ctrl+z open context menu shift+f10 source: mozilla's full shortcut reference sources and next steps this manual now has ten dedicated lessons, a final quiz, and a printable course-completion certificate. lesson completion is self-reported. related manuals: outlook , gmail , and cybersecurity . back to all manuals · back to the beginning of this manual practice this topic in mission control choose command practice or choose topic missions , then select thunderbird email. these are simulated exercises; they do not operate the actual app or account. topic missions presents a troubleshooting problem. command practice explains and checks one keyboard action at a time. use settings to choose speech and sound feedback. escape returns to the topic list during a session. when a simulator prompt says protected practice, release the modifier before the final key as instructed. in the real application, use the held keyboard combination in this manual. completing a simulation does not confirm that the real application received or performed a command. © 2026 accessible learning center

passwords and sign-in troubleshooting by symptom keyboard and control reference independent practice related learning practice this topic in mission control first-time learner: how to follow a task read the task title and its starting location before pressing anything. a keyboard command acts on the active application and focused control. merely having these instructions visible does not make the other application active. keep these instructions available. open the application separately. on windows, hold alt, tap tab to choose its window, and release alt. check the window title before continuing. focus is the place receiving your next keystroke. a screen reader announces its name and role; a visible border or highlight may mark it. tab selects the next keyboard-accessible control. shift+tab reverses that movement. neither command means “activate.” at a button or link, press enter to activate. a checkbox is an on/off choice: space changes it. listen for checked or not checked. in an open menu, use arrows to select an item, then enter. escape usually closes that menu; it does not universally return to the previous page. at a text field, enter only the requested information. ctrl+a selects all text in that field ; typing then replaces it. confirm focus before doing this. use left and right to review a small correction, or backspace to remove the character before the cursor. after opening a dialog, listen to its title, read its instructions, and tab through its controls. use cancel if you are unsure. do not repeatedly activate a button while a page or file is loading. at the result checkpoint, stop. say what changed. if the result is different, use that task’s recovery paragraph before attempting the next task. with a screen reader, arrow-key reading and text editing can use different modes. if letters become navigation commands instead of text, confirm you reached an editable field and consult your reader’s forms/focus-mode instructions in the screen readers manual . do not turn the reader off to solve an unidentified focus problem. when a task says to locate a named control, start with tab or shift+tab and listen to each complete label and role. tab skips ordinary paragraphs. if the page itself needs to be read, use your screen reader’s reading commands. if you pass the same controls twice without finding the requested one, stop and check the application, page, account, and open dialogs. a fixed number of tab presses is unreliable because layouts change. recording progress: write down the task, your starting location, the result, and one step to practice again. these activities are optional and repeatable; they are not a sequence of locked lessons. before you begin choose one practice task at a time. have your usual accessibility tools running and a way to record which steps helped. use a familiar, non-sensitive document or book for the first exercise. keyboard directions a plus sign means hold the first key while tapping the final key, then release both. for three-key combinations, hold both modifiers while tapping the last key. do not type the plus sign. “then” means release the first command before pressing the next key. tab moves forward through controls; shift+tab moves backward. enter activates a focused link or button; space commonly operates buttons and checkboxes. arrow keys move within menus and lists. pause after each step to check where focus went. for screen-reader reading and interaction modes, see the screen readers manual . phone gestures are covered in the iphone and ipad voiceover and android talkback manuals. understand the browser before navigating browser and website firefox is the application. a website is content it displays. the firefox menu changes browser behavior; a website’s menu changes that website. window and tab a window can contain several tabs. only one tab is active in that window. closing a tab is different from going back a page. address bar and page search the address bar opens an address or performs a web search. find searches words in the current page. a website’s search field searches that site’s own collection. download and bookmark a download saves a file. a bookmark saves a way to return to a page; it does not normally save a readable offline copy. browser zoom and screen magnification browser zoom changes page layout and size. a screen magnifier enlarges the computer’s display, including browser controls. you may use both, but change one at a time while learning. open firefox and establish your starting point start here: windows, with firefox installed. if needed, obtain it through firefox’s official website and follow the installer; a managed computer may need administrator help. step-by-step instructions press the windows key, type firefox, check the application name in the results, and press enter. if a first-run screen appears, read each choice before accepting it; account sign-in is separate from simply browsing. confirm the active window is firefox. press ctrl+l and enter https://accessiblelearningcenter.org/manuals.html, then enter. wait for the page to load. read the page heading using your usual reading method. tab through its interactive controls. notice that pressing tab does not read every paragraph. keep this page in one tab while using a separate tab for exercises. before entering a command, name which tab should receive it. check your result you know which application and page are active and can return to a familiar starting address. if something goes wrong if you land in a web-search results page, check the address you entered. if another browser opens, return to the windows application search and explicitly choose firefox. try it yourself open the manuals page twice from a blank tab, then explain how you verified the destination. documentation: firefox on windows installation . 1. open a page and find text what you will learn: separate the address bar from page content. exactly how to do it in firefox on windows, press ctrl+l. type accessiblelearningcenter.org and press enter. use tab to explore links. activate manuals with enter. press ctrl+f, type thunderbird, then press escape to close find. what should happen: the manual title is located on the page. if that does not happen: if you typed into the wrong control, return to the address bar and identify the page before retrying. practice: find a topic you know. explain the difference between searching this page and searching the entire web. source: mozilla keyboard shortcuts . 2. work with two tabs what you will learn: keep your instructions available while opening another page. exactly how to do it press ctrl+t and open a second familiar website. use ctrl+page up or ctrl+page down to move between adjacent tabs. close the practice tab with ctrl+w. reopen it with ctrl+shift+t. what should happen: you can return to both pages. if that does not happen: confirm the active tab before closing it; closing the final tab may close the window. practice: describe which page you expect before switching, then verify the title. source: mozilla tab shortcuts . 3. save and return to a useful page start here: the page you want to keep, open in firefox. step-by-step instructions press ctrl+d. if a bookmark editor appears, tab through its controls and locate the name field. give the bookmark a recognizable name such as “learning center — firefox.” review the folder/location choice. choose a location you will recognize, then activate save. if the page was already bookmarked, the editor may offer editing instead of a new save. open the bookmark library with ctrl+shift+o. tab to its search bookmarks field, enter part of your saved name, and move to the matching results. select the intended bookmark with arrow keys and press enter to open it. confirm the page heading or address matches what you saved. to rename or remove a practice bookmark, select it in the library and use shift+f10 to explore its context menu. read the selected action before activating it. removing a bookmark removes your saved link, not the website. check your result you can close the original tab and still return through the saved bookmark. if something goes wrong if there is no match, clear the search and check its spelling and saved location. a website’s own search box is not the bookmark library search. try it yourself save two pages with distinct names, close their original tabs, and reopen each through the library. documentation: mozilla bookmarks . 4. download a file and find the saved copy start here: a page offering a harmless document you recognize. know whether you want to save it or only view it. step-by-step instructions tab to the document’s download link and activate it. some document links first open a viewer; if so, locate that viewer’s labeled download control. if a save dialog appears, read its current folder and file name. choose a destination you can find, such as downloads, and keep a meaningful filename. activate save. if no dialog appears, the browser may use its configured default folder. open the downloads list with ctrl+j. select the expected item and check whether it is complete, still transferring, or failed. for a completed item, explore its available actions with tab or its context menu. use the action that opens the containing folder to see the saved file in file explorer. check the filename and extension before opening it. if windows asks which application to use, identify the file type rather than selecting an unrelated program. close the file and return to its folder independently. explain where the local copy is stored. clearing a browser download-history entry is different from deleting that file. check your result you can locate the completed file after leaving its original web page. if something goes wrong do not repeatedly download while an existing transfer is still in progress. a failed or blocked transfer needs its status examined. if a duplicate filename has a number added, verify which copy is the one you intend to use. try it yourself record the destination folder and filename, then locate the file without using the original website. documentation: mozilla downloads and file actions . 5. make a page easier to see what you will learn: adjust page size without changing every windows application. exactly how to do it press ctrl+plus to enlarge the page. press ctrl+minus to reduce it. press ctrl+0 to return to the normal zoom level. for text-only zoom, open the view menu with the keyboard, find zoom, and select zoom text only. compare the result on a familiar page. what should happen: you can choose a readable size and return to the baseline. if that does not happen: a very large setting may change the layout. reduce it one step and check whether content becomes easier to follow. practice: compare one heading, one paragraph, and one button at two sizes. choose the size that helps you complete the task, not simply the largest one. source: mozilla accessibility features . 6. recover when navigation feels wrong what you will learn: identify focus before changing browser settings. exactly how to do it name the problem: wrong page, wrong tab, wrong field, or unexpected reading behavior. if an unwanted find bar is active, close it with escape. if you closed the wrong tab, reopen it using the command above. if arrow keys move a text cursor through the page, check whether caret browsing was enabled with f7. read its prompt before changing it. what should happen: you can explain what changed and take one targeted recovery step. if that does not happen: check your screen reader’s current mode. do not reset the browser or delete your profile to solve an unidentified focus problem. practice: ask an instructor to move focus to the address bar. identify the change before entering any text. source: mozilla caret browsing guidance . fill in a web form without losing your place start here: a familiar website with a harmless search form. do not practice with a checkout or application that submits real information. step-by-step instructions read the form’s heading and instructions first. use tab to reach its search edit field. listen for the field’s label and whether it is required. type a distinctive topic such as firefox. if existing text needs replacing, confirm focus remains inside the edit field, press ctrl+a, and type the replacement. tab to the search button and press enter. some forms submit when you press enter in a text field, so use the labeled button when you are learning the layout. on a form with a checkbox, listen to its current checked state, then use space only if you intend to change it. for a list of options, use its arrow-key choices and confirm the selected value before leaving it. after submitting, read the new heading, result count, or validation error. if a field is rejected, return to that labeled field and correct only the indicated value. when finished, leave the form through its ordinary navigation. do not assume escape undoes a submission or that the browser back command will preserve unsaved text. check your result the intended form action occurs once, and you can identify its result or error message. if something goes wrong if a single letter moves to a heading instead of appearing in the field, your screen reader may still be reading the page. re-identify the editable field and use your reader’s interaction instructions. if audio or a dialog interrupts you, identify it before continuing. try it yourself search for a manual, replace the search word with another topic, and describe which field changed. documentation: firefox accessibility . read an article in reader view start here: a text-heavy article in firefox on windows. reader view is not available for every page. step-by-step instructions press f9 to request reader view. if your laptop assigns another action to its function keys, use the keyboard’s appropriate function-key mode or use firefox’s view menu and its reader view command. read the simplified page heading and a paragraph. tab to the reader view controls to explore its appearance options. adjust one text or appearance setting, then return to the article and compare the result. choose a size that lets you track a full line comfortably. use the reader view exit control or return to the original page. check that you are back at the website before trying its ordinary navigation. check your result on a supported article, you get a simpler reading presentation and can return to the original. if something goes wrong if reader view is unavailable, use ordinary page zoom and your screen reader’s reading navigation. do not expect account forms, dashboards, or every pdf to convert into an article. try it yourself compare the same paragraph in the original page and reader view. explain which presentation makes it easier to follow. documentation: mozilla reader view . understand saved passwords and sign-in start here: firefox on your own trusted device. use a practice account if you are learning password controls. step-by-step instructions open firefox’s application menu and activate passwords, or type about:logins in the address bar and press enter. this opens firefox’s saved-login manager, not a website’s password-reset page. tab to its search field and search for a site you recognize. select the matching entry and review its website and username. do not reveal or copy a password merely to identify the entry. if you intentionally request a protected action, windows may ask you to authenticate. if you edit a saved entry, understand that you are changing firefox’s stored copy. to change the actual account password, follow that website’s own account-recovery or security process, then update the saved copy as appropriate. close the login-manager tab when finished. on shared devices, follow the device owner’s sign-in and password-storage policy. check your result you can distinguish a stored credential from the website account itself. if something goes wrong a rejected login may be an old saved password, a different account, or a site-specific access problem. verify the website address and username before requesting recovery. do not repeatedly guess passwords. try it yourself identify the manager’s search field and website field without displaying or sharing any secret. documentation: mozilla saved-login manager . troubleshooting by symptom the wrong page opened. read its address and title. return to the known starting address if necessary. a similar-looking search result is not proof that it is the official site. the page looks cut off after zooming. reduce browser zoom one step and check whether a menu has collapsed into a menu button. if screen magnification is also active, identify which zoom you changed. my text vanished. check the active tab and focused field before retyping. a form may have navigated away. use its saved-draft feature where provided; browser history is not a reliable backup of form text. a keyboard command does nothing. check for an open menu, dialog, screen-reader command conflict, or laptop function-key behavior. return focus to the intended control and try once. record the command and what happened if the problem continues. i hear two voices. identify whether the website or a media player is speaking alongside your screen reader. pause that player through its controls before changing the screen reader you rely on for navigation. keyboard and control reference windows browser commands task command address bar ctrl+l new tab ctrl+t close / reopen tab ctrl+w / ctrl+shift+t previous / next adjacent tab ctrl+page up / ctrl+page down find text ctrl+f bookmark page ctrl+d bookmark library ctrl+shift+o downloads ctrl+j reader view on a supported article f9 (windows) reset page zoom ctrl+0 open selected item’s context menu shift+f10 source: mozilla shortcut reference . independent practice choose any activity; there is no required order or passing score. open the manuals page and find a named topic. keep two manuals in separate tabs and switch between them. bookmark one manual, close its tab, and return using the bookmark. find a downloaded practice file on your computer. explain whether an access problem belongs to the browser, the website, or your screen-reader mode. after each task, record whether you completed it independently, needed a prompt, or want another attempt. repeat the difficult step instead of restarting everything. related learning continue with the chrome , edge , or cybersecurity manual. this manual now has ten dedicated lessons, a final quiz, and a printable course-completion certificate. lesson completion is self-reported. back to all manuals · back to the beginning practice this topic in mission control choose command practice or choose topic missions , then select firefox. these are simulated exercises; they do not operate the actual app or account. topic missions presents a troubleshooting problem. command practice explains and checks one keyboard action at a time. use settings to choose speech and sound feedback. escape returns to the topic list during a session. when a simulator prompt says protected practice, release the modifier before the final key as instructed. in the real application, use the held keyboard combination in this manual. completing a simulation does not confirm that the real application received or performed a command. © 2026 accessible learning center

windows tasks. start lesson 1 all ten lessons final quiz and certificate back to all manuals · search learning resources for installed zoomtext or fusion on windows. start with the product and keyboard-layout check below. default commands may have been customized on your computer. documentation checked september 17, 2026. these instructions have not been tested here with the actual windows assistive software or a signed-in reading-service account. control names can vary by version. follow the label you hear rather than counting tab presses. first-time learner: how to follow a task before you begin understand what is being enlarged or spoken 1. identify your product and layout prepare a usable setup before changing preferences 2. start fusion and locate its controls 3. choose useful magnification 4. improve pointer, cursor, and focus visibility 5. set a comfortable listening pace 6. practice a complete work task operate the zoomtext toolbar with the keyboard follow text while reading and editing read with fusion: separate jaws speech from magnification manage speech while switching between applications recover by identifying the symptom keyboard and control reference independent practice related learning practice this topic in mission control first-time learner: how to follow a task read the task title and its starting location before pressing anything. a keyboard command acts on the active application and focused control. merely having these instructions visible does not make the other application active. keep these instructions available. open the application separately. on windows, hold alt, tap tab to choose its window, and release alt. check the window title before continuing. focus is the place receiving your next keystroke. a screen reader announces its name and role; a visible border or highlight may mark it. tab selects the next keyboard-accessible control. shift+tab reverses that movement. neither command means “activate.” at a button or link, press enter to activate. a checkbox is an on/off choice: space changes it. listen for checked or not checked. in an open menu, use arrows to select an item, then enter. escape usually closes that menu; it does not universally return to the previous page. at a text field, enter only the requested information. ctrl+a selects all text in that field ; typing then replaces it. confirm focus before doing this. use left and right to review a small correction, or backspace to remove the character before the cursor. after opening a dialog, listen to its title, read its instructions, and tab through its controls. use cancel if you are unsure. do not repeatedly activate a button while a page or file is loading. at the result checkpoint, stop. say what changed. if the result is different, use that task’s recovery paragraph before attempting the next task. with a screen reader, arrow-key reading and text editing can use different modes. if letters become navigation commands instead of text, confirm you reached an editable field and consult your reader’s forms/focus-mode instructions in the screen readers manual . do not turn the reader off to solve an unidentified focus problem. when a task says to locate a named control, start with tab or shift+tab and listen to each complete label and role. tab skips ordinary paragraphs. if the page itself needs to be read, use your screen reader’s reading commands. if you pass the same controls twice without finding the requested one, stop and check the application, page, account, and open dialogs. a fixed number of tab presses is unreliable because layouts change. recording progress: write down the task, your starting location, the result, and one step to practice again. these activities are optional and repeatable; they are not a sequence of locked lessons. before you begin choose one practice task at a time. have your usual accessibility tools running and a way to record which steps helped. use a familiar, non-sensitive document or book for the first exercise. keyboard directions a plus sign means hold the first key while tapping the final key, then release both. for three-key combinations, hold both modifiers while tapping the last key. do not type the plus sign. “then” means release the first command before pressing the next key. tab moves forward through controls; shift+tab moves backward. enter activates a focused link or button; space commonly operates buttons and checkboxes. arrow keys move within menus and lists. pause after each step to check where focus went. for screen-reader reading and interaction modes, see the screen readers manual . phone gestures are covered in the iphone and ipad voiceover and android talkback manuals. understand what is being enlarged or spoken magnification level the enlargement factor. at higher levels, less of the desktop fits in the visible area. a larger number is useful only if you can still track your task. pointer, cursor, and focus the pointer follows the mouse. the text cursor marks where typing will appear. keyboard focus identifies the control receiving a key. they can be in three different places. tracking the enlarged view follows a changing location, such as typing or keyboard focus. if the display moves unexpectedly, first identify what received focus. speech and screen reading speech reads information aloud. a full screen reader also provides navigation and information about controls. zoomtext magnifier alone does not provide the reader features of magnifier/reader. fusion combines magnification with jaws screen reading. keyboard layout the configured command layout, such as jaws desktop or laptop. it is not necessarily determined by the physical shape of the keyboard. documentation: zoomtext product differences and fusion product differences . 1. identify your product and layout what you will learn: choose the instructions that match the installed software. exactly how to do it find the installed product name and version in its help or about information. record whether it is zoomtext magnifier, zoomtext magnifier/reader, or fusion. for fusion, confirm whether jaws is configured for desktop or laptop keyboard layout. keyboard shape alone does not identify the configured layout. use the matching command column below. ask your instructor to check the layout if you are unsure. what should happen: you know which magnification and speech instructions apply. if that does not happen: do not assume a missing reading feature is a fault: zoomtext editions differ, and fusion uses jaws for screen reading. practice: explain your product name and which tool supplies speech. source: zoomtext editions . source: fusion layout and speech differences . prepare a usable setup before changing preferences start here: windows with the licensed product installed. keep your existing access method available while checking a new setup. step-by-step instructions identify the installed application by its name in windows start: zoomtext or fusion. if neither is installed, use the official zoomtext downloads or your organization’s approved fusion installer. installation and activation may need an administrator. launch only the intended product for this exercise. in its interface, open help or about using the keyboard-accessible menu and record the name and version. record whether you have magnification only, magnifier/reader, or fusion. for fusion, identify the configured jaws keyboard layout before using the two-column command table below. if you do not know it, use the labeled toolbar controls while you check the installed help or ask the person who configured the device. open a short, non-sensitive text document with a heading and two paragraphs. put these instructions in a separate window so you can switch back using alt+tab. write down the current magnification level and speech setting before making changes. change one setting, inspect the result, and restore it if it makes the exercise harder. check your result you have a known product, a practice document, and a recorded baseline to return to. if something goes wrong if two programs speak simultaneously, identify which products are running before closing either one. do not shut down the only tool providing access to the screen. ask for setup help if the product or layout remains unclear. try it yourself state your product, its speech capability, and the starting magnification level before continuing. documentation: zoomtext getting started · fusion getting started . 2. start fusion and locate its controls what you will learn: reach the application without relying on a tiny mouse target. exactly how to do it with fusion installed, locate its desktop shortcut using the keyboard and press enter. inspect the fusion interface: magnifier, reader, and tools tabs provide its controls. on the reader tab, locate voice and rate. adjust one setting, then return to your practice document. what should happen: magnification and speech are available together. if that does not happen: if fusion does not start, report the exact launch or licensing message; do not repeatedly start additional copies. practice: locate the magnification and speech controls separately. change only one and describe the effect. source: getting started with fusion . 3. choose useful magnification what you will learn: balance readable text with enough surrounding context. exactly how to do it in zoomtext or fusion desktop layout, use caps lock+up to increase zoom and caps lock+down to decrease it. fusion laptop layout adds alt to these combinations. use the matching 1x toggle in the table below to compare the enlarged view with the whole screen. return to your preferred size and read a short paragraph. what should happen: you can locate both the text and the surrounding controls. if that does not happen: if a command reads text instead, stop and check the fusion keyboard layout. do not keep repeating it. practice: find a heading, move to a paragraph, then find a nearby button. note which zoom level made all three easiest. source: zoomtext magnification . source: fusion magnification layouts . 4. improve pointer, cursor, and focus visibility what you will learn: understand three different visual targets. exactly how to do it in zoomtext, use caps lock+p to toggle pointer enhancement, caps lock+r for the text cursor, and caps lock+f for focus enhancement. test the pointer by moving the mouse, the text cursor by editing practice text, and focus by tabbing among buttons. toggle each feature again to compare before deciding what helps. what should happen: you can distinguish the mouse pointer, editing position, and selected control. if that does not happen: a text-cursor enhancement cannot locate a mouse pointer. first identify which target you are trying to follow. practice: type “my next appointment is friday.” find the editing position, then tab to a control and identify the focus marker. source: zoomtext enhancement commands . 5. set a comfortable listening pace what you will learn: use the correct speech controls for your product. exactly how to do it in zoomtext magnifier/reader, caps lock+alt+up or down changes voice rate. control briefly quiets speech. in fusion, use the reader tab’s voice and rate controls. jaws supplies speech; zoomtext reading hotkeys are not interchangeable with fusion speech commands. listen to one short passage, adjust one step, and compare comprehension. what should happen: you can understand the spoken material without repeatedly losing your place. if that does not happen: check the product edition, audio output, and voice setting before increasing volume. if another screen reader is also speaking, identify it before changing anything. practice: summarize a short paragraph at two rates. keep the rate at which you understand and navigate comfortably. source: zoomtext speech settings . source: fusion reader controls . source: fusion speech source . 6. practice a complete work task what you will learn: move between overview, detail, and speech deliberately. exactly how to do it open a familiar practice document. choose a readable magnification level. locate its heading, read a paragraph, and find one named word. move to another application and back. identify the current control before typing. record the product, keyboard layout, zoom level, and speech preference that worked. what should happen: your setup supports a complete task, not only a larger picture. if that does not happen: when a change makes the task harder, reverse that one change. avoid changing color, zoom, and voice together because you will not know which helped. practice: repeat with a webpage. compare whether the same setup works equally well in both applications. this is an original practice routine; use the official command references below for your installed version. operate the zoomtext toolbar with the keyboard start here: the zoomtext toolbar is the active window. these toolbar directions are for zoomtext; use fusion’s own controls when running fusion. step-by-step instructions identify the toolbar tab or control that has focus. use the arrow keys to move among toolbar items. listen to the control name before activating it. at a split button, distinguish its two actions: enter operates its main function, while down opens its associated choices. read the choices before selecting one. at the zoom level control, use up or down to change the level. use left or right to leave that control for adjacent toolbar items. switch to the practice document with alt+tab and inspect one heading and one line of text. return to the toolbar to make another small adjustment only if needed. when a settings menu opens unexpectedly, use escape to close that menu and identify the focused toolbar item again. check your result you can use controls by their labels and roles instead of searching for a small visual target. if something goes wrong if arrow keys change the level instead of moving to another item, you may be inside the zoom level control. use left or right to leave it. if the document scrolls instead, the document has focus rather than the toolbar. try it yourself reach zoom level, change it one step, and return it to the value you recorded. documentation: freedom scientific zoomtext toolbar navigation . follow text while reading and editing start here: your practice document at a comfortable enlargement. the document’s edit area has focus. step-by-step instructions read the heading, then move to the first paragraph using your usual text-navigation method. pause when the enlarged view moves and identify which line is now visible. type a short sentence at a known insertion point. watch or listen for where each word appears. if you cannot locate it, stop typing and identify the cursor before adding more text. compare pointer enhancement by moving the mouse, cursor enhancement by moving within the text, and focus enhancement by using tab in a dialog. these are separate tests, not interchangeable effects. if a line is too wide to follow comfortably, reduce magnification one step or adjust the document’s layout. compare comprehension and effort before increasing it again. use your product/layout’s 1x comparison command from the reference table to orient to the full screen, then return to your working view. do not change the operating system’s display resolution as a substitute for this exercise. check your result you know whether you are following the mouse, text cursor, or keyboard focus, and can regain context after the enlarged view moves. if something goes wrong if typing appears in the wrong application, use alt+tab and confirm the document title. if the text is correct but difficult to see, adjust the appropriate visual setting rather than repeatedly retyping it. try it yourself add and correct one sentence, then locate the document’s save control without losing your place. documentation: zoomtext enhancement controls · fusion layout-specific controls . read with fusion: separate jaws speech from magnification start here: fusion is running, its jaws keyboard layout is known, and a short document is active. step-by-step instructions use the command table below to choose the correct desktop or laptop command. do not borrow a zoomtext reader command just because its name sounds similar: fusion uses jaws speech. for continuous reading in desktop layout, use insert+down arrow. in laptop layout, use caps lock+down arrow. hold the modifier while pressing the arrow; release both after the command. press control to interrupt speech. check where the reading or editing position is before moving to another passage. for the current line, desktop layout uses insert+up arrow; laptop layout uses caps lock+i. read the line once, then move deliberately to the next passage using the document’s navigation. to adjust speed without guessing another product’s shortcut, return to fusion’s reader controls and locate rate. change it a small amount, return to the same paragraph, and compare. when reading is done, leave speech at a useful setting. stopping the current utterance is different from disabling ongoing speech feedback. check your result you can start reading, stop it, and hear the current line using commands appropriate to your configured fusion layout. if something goes wrong if a command magnifies instead of speaking, recheck the configured layout. caps lock combinations have different meanings in these products and layouts. if there is no speech, inspect the reader voice control and windows audio output before reinstalling anything. try it yourself read a paragraph, interrupt halfway, then request the current line. describe where you are before resuming. documentation: fusion keyboard layouts and speech commands . manage speech while switching between applications start here: your practice document and a browser are open. use the product-specific speech section above to set a comfortable rate. step-by-step instructions read one paragraph, then stop the current speech before switching windows. this lets you hear the next window’s title instead of overlapping explanations. use alt+tab to switch. identify the destination application, active document or page, and focused control before using a command. if a web page or audiobook also plays audio, pause that media player through its own labeled control. keep the access tool you need to navigate available. return to the document and locate your last passage using a heading, distinctive phrase, or your recorded place. read a short portion to confirm context. for zoomtext magnifier/reader, inspect its reader settings if character or mouse announcements are distracting. change one echo setting and test typing or pointer movement separately. for fusion, use the corresponding jaws controls rather than assuming those zoomtext speech settings apply. check your result you can tell which source is speaking and switch tasks without losing your place. if something goes wrong if everything is silent, check volume, output device, and the product’s voice setting separately. plugging in headphones can change the output device. a moving highlight alone does not prove that audio is reaching your speakers. try it yourself switch between a document and the manuals page twice, identify each destination, and return to the same paragraph. documentation: zoomtext speech and echo controls · fusion reader controls . recover by identifying the symptom i cannot see the whole window. compare the full-screen view using the matching 1x toggle, then return to a lower working magnification if needed. find the window and focused control before changing more settings. a highlight follows the wrong thing. check whether it is the pointer, text cursor, or keyboard focus. test only the corresponding enhancement. a mouse highlight will not tell you where typed text goes. the same key behaves differently on another computer. compare the product, version, and configured keyboard layout. copying someone else’s command list without matching these details can produce another action. a document image has no readable text. a scanned page may need text recognition, often called ocr. fusion can support recognition workflows, including supported scanned-pdf workflows. follow the recognition prompt or installed help; recognition output must be checked for errors, especially numbers and names. the program does not start after windows sign-in. open it through start first. then review its startup preference with the person managing the computer. do not enable multiple overlapping access tools automatically without checking the resulting startup experience. when requesting help, provide the product/version, keyboard layout, application, exact command, expected result, and actual result. do not include private document text. documentation: fusion recognition and product guidance . keyboard and control reference magnification: choose the correct layout task zoomtext / fusion desktop fusion laptop increase / decrease zoom caps lock+up / down caps lock+alt+up / down toggle current zoom and 1x caps lock+enter caps lock+alt+enter toggle color enhancement caps lock+c caps lock+alt+c source: zoomtext hotkeys . source: fusion hotkeys . for zoomtext toolbar controls, arrow keys navigate. on a split button, enter toggles the feature and down opens its settings. in zoom level, up and down adjust the value. source: zoomtext toolbar navigation . independent practice choose any activity; there is no required order or passing score. identify your installed product and configured keyboard layout. find a button at your preferred zoom, then compare the whole-screen view. explain pointer versus text cursor versus keyboard focus. read and summarize a paragraph with a comfortable speech rate. troubleshoot an unexpected command by checking product and layout before changing preferences. after each task, record whether you completed it independently, needed a prompt, or want another attempt. repeat the difficult step instead of restarting everything. related learning see windows accessibility for built-in alternatives and screen readers for jaws reading practice. this manual now has ten dedicated lessons, a final quiz, and a printable course-completion certificate. lesson completion is self-reported. back to all manuals · back to the beginning practice this topic in mission control choose command practice or choose topic missions , then select zoomtext and fusion. these are simulated exercises; they do not operate the actual app or account. topic missions presents a troubleshooting problem. command practice explains and checks one keyboard action at a time. use settings to choose speech and sound feedback. escape returns to the topic list during a session. when a simulator prompt says protected practice, release the modifier before the final key as instructed. in the real application, use the held keyboard combination in this manual. completing a simulation does not confirm that the real application received or performed a command. © 2026 accessible learning center
